catalog_citation: Gordon, Matthew (2004). A phonological and phonetic study of word-level stress in Chickasaw. International Journal of American Linguistics 70(1): 1-32. DOI 10.1086/422264. Corroborated by Gordon, Matthew K. (2005). Intonational phonology of Chickasaw. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology, 301-330. Oxford: OUP (sec. 11.2.2, p. 303) and Gordon, Matthew (2003). catalog_locator: Gordon 2004: abstract p. 1; sec. 4.1 'Words with one or no long vowels' p. 7; sec. 4.2 pp. 19-21; sec. 5.2 'Metrical analysis' p. 25; sec. 5.3 'Syllable weight' pp. 26-27; sec. 6 'Summary' p. 27).
catalog_quote: The location of stress is phonologically predictable, falling on word-final syllables, heavy (CVC and CVV) syllables, and on the second in a sequence of light (CV) syllables. Short vowels in nonfinal open syllables are made heavy through a process of rhythmic vowel lengthening. Primary stress is sensitive to a further weight distinction, which treats CVV as heavier than both CV and CVC. In words lacking a CVV syllable, stress falls on the final syllable. ... The present data further suggest a weight distinction between CVC and CVV for primary stress at the word level. Stress falls on a CVV syllable if one occurs in the word. In words lacking a long vowel, primary stress falls on the final syllable, even if the final syllable is CV and there is a nonfinal CVC. ... If present, CVV carries prominence on the primary stress tier; otherwise, the final syllable carries an additional grid mark in words lacking a CVV syllable. ... The measured data provide support for a typologically unusual system of weight-sensitive stress. Stress falls on heavy syllables, i.e., long vowels and closed syllables, as well as on final syllables. Primary stress falls on the final syllable unless there is a long vowel, which carries primary stress even in nonfinal position. Primary stress in words with two long vowels is subject to free variation, falling on either one or both of the long vowels.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Chickasaw (chic1270) is not in the catalog. All three Glottolog-listed Gordon items were obtained as open author copies from Matthew Gordon's UCSB faculty page (Google Drive links) and read; a fourth supporting paper (Gordon, Munro & Ladefoged 2000) was downloaded too. Bibliographic corrections: Glottolog 182617 lists the 2003 paper under 'Afrika und Übersee' but it is Phonology 20(2):173-218 (DOI 10.1017/S0952675703004512); the 2005 chapter was published as 'Intonational Phonology of Chickasaw' (Prosodic Typology, OUP, pp. 301-330, DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199249633.003.0011). Consistent statement across all sources: word stress is predictable and weight-sensitive; secondary stress on all heavy syllables (CVC, CVV incl. rhythmically lengthened second-of-two-light vowels) and on all word-final syllables; primary stress on the (rightmost) CVV if any, else on the final syllable; multi-CVV words show free variation. Phrase-final words are instead governed by the phrasal pitch accent (final in statements; final CVV/heavy penult/antepenult in questions). Best first-hand statement: Gordon 2004 IJAL (acoustic study, 8 speakers), with. Nothing remains unacquired; no acquisition priorities.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress is predictable and weight-sensitive with a three-way hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV. Every heavy syllable (CVC, phonemic CVV, and rhythmically lengthened CV, i.e. the second of two consecutive non-final open syllables) and every word-final syllable carries at least secondary stress. Primary stress goes to the long/lengthened vowel (CVV) if the word has exactly one; if there is none, primary stress is on the final syllable (even a light CV final syllable when a CVC precedes). Gordon 2005 (p. 303) states the multi-CVV case as rightmost long/lengthened vowel; Gordon 2003 says 'most commonly the rightmost CVV'; Gordon 2004 (pp. 19-21, 27) reports free inter- and intra-speaker variation (first, second, or both CVV) in words with two long vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: three acoustically distinguished levels (primary, secondary, unstressed). All non-primary heavy syllables (CVC, CVV, rhythmically lengthened vowels) and non-primary final syllables carry secondary stress; cues are f0, duration and intensity, with duration the most reliable (pp. 8-17, 23-24).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with two or more long vowels show free variation in primary-stress location (either or both CVV). Rhythmic lengthening skips word-final syllables and certain affixes (e.g. dative im- lies outside the lengthening domain, Gordon 2005 p. 303). Stress is described as not phonemic (Gordon 2005 p. 303). Lexical/morphological 'grade' pitch accents coexist with stress and are independent of it (Gordon 2004 sec. 2.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in words that are NOT final in an Intonational Phrase (elicited in carrier phrases). IP-final words (including isolation/citation forms) instead carry the nuclear pitch accent: final syllable in statements; in questions final CVV, else heavy penult, else antepenult (Gordon 2003; 2004 p. 4). Gordon 1999 suggests the statement-final H% boundary tone underlies the impression of final stress. Chickasaw is also a lexical pitch accent ('grade') language; Gordon 2004 treats it as having both stress and pitch accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Chickasaw (chic1270, ISO cic) as spoken in south-central Oklahoma; data from 8 elder speakers recorded 1996-2002. No dialect distinction is made. Note that Glottolog ref 182617 (Gordon 2003) is mis-attributed to Afrika und Übersee; the article is in Phonology 20(2).

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, quantity-based system with a bounded (iambic) rhythmic component: secondary stress on every heavy syllable (CVC and CVV, the latter including rhythmically lengthened second-of-two-lights) and on every word-final syllable; primary stress on a CVV syllable if the word contains one (rightmost CVV most commonly, with free variation when there are several), otherwise on the final syllable. Word-level rule holds for phrase-medial words; phrase-final words take the phrasal pitch accent instead (final in statements; final CVV > heavy penult > antepenult in questions, per Gordon 2003). Acoustically established with 8 speakers; speakers lack stress intuitions. Chickasaw is not in the catalog, so this would be the deciding source for a new record (kind: weight-sensitive / unbounded-to-rightmost-CVV with final default).

sources.quote: The measured data provide support for a typologically unusual system of weight-sensitive stress. Stress falls on heavy syllables, i.e., long vowels and closed syllables, as well as on final syllables. Primary stress falls on the final syllable unless there is a long vowel, which carries primary stress even in nonfinal position. Primary stress in words with two long vowels is subject to free variation, falling on either one or both of the long vowels. [p. 7:] Stress falls on a CVV syllable if one occurs in the word. In words lacking a long vowel, primary stress falls on the final syllable, even if the final syllable is CV and there is a nonfinal CVC.
sources.locator: Section 6 'Summary', p. 27; fuller phonological statement in section 4.1, p. 7 (bracketed sentence); multi-CVV variation section 4.2, pp. 19-21
sources.note: weight-sensitive: all heavy syllables (CVC, CVV incl. rhythmically lengthened) and all word-final syllables are stressed; primary stress on the CVV if the word has one (CVV > CVC), otherwise on the final syllable; with two or more CVV, primary stress varies freely (rightmost, leftmost, or both). Three acoustically distinct stress levels (pp. 7, 19-21, 27).

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew (2003). The phonology of pitch accents in Chickasaw. Phonology 20(2): 173-218. [Glottolog 182617 gives the venue as Afrika und Übersee; the paper itself and Crossref give Phonology 20]
sources.quote: Word-level stress in Chickasaw in Chickasaw is phonologically predictable. It falls on the final syllable of a word, on heavy syllables (CVV and CVC), and on the second in a sequence of light (CV) syllables. A stressed vowel in a non-final CV syllable is rhythmically lengthened ... In IP-non-final words, the final syllable carries primary stress in words lacking either a long or rhythmically lengthened vowel. In words containing a single long (or lengthened vowel), henceforth CVV, the primary stress falls on the long/lengthened vowel. In words containing multiple CVV syllables, there is variation, both inter and intraspeaker, in whether the rightmost or leftmost CVV carries primary stress. Most commonly, the rightmost CVV receives primary stress
sources.locator: section 2 'Chickasaw stress', preprint pp. 2-3 (journal pp. ~175-176); section 1 preprint p. 2
sources.note: Same word-level rule as Gordon 2004 (secondary stress on heavies and finals; primary on the single CVV, else final; with multiple CVV usually rightmost, variable). Adds the phrase-level picture: in IP-final words the phrasal pitch accent overrides word stress — final syllable in statements, but in questions the accent (and primary stress) goes to a final CVV, else a heavy penult, else the antepenult (e.g. /a:Soppala?/ 'lamp': initial stress medially, final in statements, antepenult in questions). sources.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Chickasaw; rather, the Chickasaw stress system is weight-sensitive ... With respect to stress, Munro (1996) observes that the final syllable of a word is prominent, as are closed syllables and syllables containing long vowels (including phonemic long vowels, rhythmically lengthened vowels, and nasalized vowels, all of which are phonetically long). Thus, CVV and CVC are heavier than CV, which is unstressed unless in final position. Primary stress falls on the rightmost long (or lengthened vowel) in a word, indicating that CVV is heavier than CVC. In the absence of any long vowels, the primary stress falls on the final syllable of a word.
sources.note: An intonation (ToBI-style AM) chapter; only its background section 11.2.2 treats word stress, restating the same rule as Gordon 2003/2004 (heavies and finals prominent; primary on the rightmost CVV, else the final syllable). The rest (nuclear pitch accent placement, boundary tones, phrasing) is phrase-level prosody. Only pp. 301-304 were scanned; the remaining pages are about intonation.

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew (2003). The phonology of pitch accent placement in Chickasaw. Phonology 20(2): 173-218 (author preprint; Glottolog 182617 mis-lists the venue as Afrika und Übersee)
sources.note: Section 2 'Chickasaw stress' (preprint pp. 2-3): word-level stress is phonologically predictable, on the final syllable, on heavy syllables (CVV, CVC) and on the second of two light syllables (which is rhythmically lengthened); in IP-non-final words primary stress is on the sole CVV, else on the final syllable; with multiple CVV, variation, most commonly rightmost CVV primary. IP-final words instead carry the nuclear pitch accent (final syllable in statements; final CVV / heavy penult / antepenult in questions).

sources.note: 'Prosody' paragraph (p. 289): not tonal but 'grades' carry a high pitch accent; phonemic long and lengthened vowels tend to be more prominent; in isolated words lacking long/lengthened vowels the final syllable has the greatest amplitude and highest f0.

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew, Pamela Munro & Peter Ladefoged (2000). Some phonetic structures of Chickasaw. Anthropological Linguistics 42(3): 366-400. [not in the works with stress in the title list; supporting source downloaded from Gordon's page]
sources.quote: Rhythmic lengthening is plausibly linked to the location of stress in Chickasaw. Word-final syllables, closed syllables, syllables containing long vowels, and syllables containing rhythmically lengthened vowels are realized with increased prominence which could be termed stress (Munro 1996, Munro et al. in preparation, Gordon 1999), though "stressed" syllables at the word-level are less prominent than stressed syllables at the phrase-level.
sources.locator: section 1 (Introduction), the text layerof journal p. ~368)
sources.note: Preprint pp. 2-3: word-final syllables, closed syllables, long-vowel syllables and rhythmically lengthened syllables 'are realized with increased prominence which could be termed stress (Munro 1996..)', word-level stress less prominent than phrase-level; rhythmic lengthening plausibly = lengthening of a stressed short vowel in a non-final open syllable.
